The patella, quadriceps tendon, and patellar tendon constitute the extensor mechanism of the
knee1 (Resource 1).
Disruption of any component of the extensor mechanism may lead to loss of knee function
because knee extension is required for normal gait.
Repair of the patella, quadriceps tendon, or patellar tendon is indicated if loss of extensor
mechanism function of the knee and/or an articular step-off is present.

Overview
Active knee extensor mechanism function is necessary for normal gait and for various
activities of daily living and physical activities. Disruption of the patella, quadriceps
tendon, or patellar tendon results in loss of continuity of the extensor mechanism, and
surgical management may be required. In addition, surgical management of articular
step-off of the patella may be required to minimize the risk of posttraumatic arthritis of
the patellofemoral joint.
Epidemiology
Patellar Fractures
Fractures of the patella occur most commonly in individuals aged 20 to 50 years.
The male-to-female ratio is 2:1.
Patellar fractures make up 1% of all skeletal injuries.

Patellar Fractures
Fractures of the patella represent 1% of all fractures. They most commonly occur in
individuals aged 20 to 50 years, with a 2:1 male-to-female ratio. In the most complete
epidemiologic study of patella fractures to date, Larsen et al2 reported that the incidence
of patella fractures was 13.1 in 100,000 per year between 2005 and 2014. In a cohort of
756 consecutive patella fractures studied during this time period, the most common
fracture patterns were type 34-C3 (25%) and type 34-C1 (23.2%)2 (Table 1).

Quadriceps Tendon Ruptures
Quadriceps tendon ruptures most commonly occur in adult males and African
Americans older than 40 years. Risk factors for quadriceps tendon rupture include
chronic renal failure, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes mellitus, systemic steroids,
hyperparathyroidism, gout, connective tissue disorders, obesity, and fluoroquinolone

presented to the Edinburgh Orthopaedic Trauma Unit, 36 (1.3%) of which were
quadriceps tendon ruptures, occurring at an incidence of 1.37 per 100,000 (Figure 1).

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Patella
Osteology
The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the body.
The patella has seven facets; the distal pole is termed the apex.
Bipartite patella most commonly involves the superolateral portion; the incidence in the
general population ranges from 0.2% to 6%.4

Osteology
The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the body and has seven facets. The distal
pole of the patella is termed the apex. Bipartite patella occurs in 2% to 3% of the general
population, with an equal prevalence in males and females and being bilateral in 50% of
individuals. Saupe classified bipartite patella into three groups based on the position of
the accessory center: type I, at the inferior pole (5%); type II, at the lateral margin (20%);
and type III, at the superolateral pole (75%)4 (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Drawings show the Saupe classification of bipartite patella. A, Type I: accessory
center at the inferior pole. Type II: accessory center at the lateral margin. B, Type III:
accessory center at the superolateral pole. L = lateral, M = medial. (Reproduced from
Atesok K, Doral MN, Lowe J, Finsterbush A: Symptomatic bipartite patella: Treatment
alternatives. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2008;16[8]:455-461.)

The blood supply arises from the geniculate arteries, which contribute to an arterial ring
around the patella.
The principal arterial supply enters the patella inferomedially.

Tendons
The quadriceps tendon inserts onto the superior pole of the patella.
The patellar tendon originates from the inferior pole of the patella.
Joints and Ligaments
The proximal portion of the patella is covered with the thickest articular cartilage in the body.
The distal pole is devoid of articular cartilage.
Musculature
Four separate muscles—the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, and vastus
medialis—converge and insert as a single quadriceps tendon on the proximal pole of the
patella.
The patella increases the power of the extensor mechanism 30% by anteriorly displacing it
away from the knee center of rotation (increased moment arm)6 (Figure 6).

Musculature
During knee range of motion, a differential force exists in the quadriceps and the
patellar tendon. During the first part of knee flexion, the force in the patellar tendon is
greater than the force in the quadriceps tendon. The reverse is true as the knee
continues to flex.7 During initial knee extension from a fully flexed position, up to 6,000
N of force can be generated from the transmission of force from the quadriceps through
the patella to the tibia.8 During 45° of flexion to termination to extension, the patella
displaces the tendon away from the center of rotation of the knee, increasing the
moment arm and providing a mechanical advantage that increases the force of knee
extension by as much as 50%, depending on the angle of knee flexion.5-7 (Figure 7).

Detailed anatomic studies of the patellar tendon show that the tendon vessels arise
from three main sources. Anteroproximally, the tendon primarily is supplied by the

anastomotic arch between the anterior tibial recurrent and the inferior medial genicular
arteries. Posteriorly, the tendon is supplied via the retropatellar anastomotic arch in the
infrapatella (Hoffa) fat pad12 (Figure 10).

Associated Injuries

Associated Injuries
Associated injury rates in patients with a patellar fracture range from 15% to 28%.13,14
These injuries typically involve the ipsilateral lower extremity. Associated injury rates are
almost 80% in patients with an open patella fracture.5 Among patients with a quadriceps
tendon rupture, 10% have an intra-articular knee injury.15 Among patients with a
patellar tendon rupture, 30% have an associated injury, 18% have a medial meniscus
tear, and 18% have an anterior cruciate ligament rupture.15 Distal avulsion from the
tibial tubercle is rare but associated with occult multiligamentous knee injury.16

Injury Classification

Injury Classification
The Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation fracture classification categorizes
the patella as type 34. Extra-articular fractures of the patella are classified as type 34A.
Partial articular sagittal fractures of the patella are classified as type 34B. Complete
articular fractures of the patella in the frontal/coronal plate are classified as type 34C17
(Figure 11). The descriptive classification of patellar fractures also is useful to describe
the various nuances of patella fractures. In the descriptive classification, patellar
fractures may be un-displaced, transverse, lower or upper pole, multi-fragmented
undisplaced or displaced, vertical, or osteochondral5 (Figure 12).

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients may report a pop and sudden knee instability and an inability to ambulate, with pain
localized to the knee.
Physical Examination for Suspected Extensor Mechanism Disruption
The soft tissues should be inspected carefully for lacerations, abrasions, and ecchymosis.
Extensor lag and the ability to perform a straight-leg raise should be evaluated.
The examiner should palpate for an extensor mechanism defect.
If pain limits the evaluation, intra-articular injection of local anesthetic can enable better
assessment.

Physical Examination for Suspected Extensor Mechanism Disruption
A thorough evaluation of the integrity of the extensor mechanism should be performed
in any patient with knee pain and/or swelling about the knee. After visual inspection of
the knee for abrasions, lacerations, or ecchymosis, a simple straight leg raise maneuver
should be performed. If the patient can perform the straight leg raise without an
extensor lag, then the extensor mechanism likely is in continuity. If the patient is unable
to perform the straight leg raise against gravity, the patient can be placed on his or her
side with the injured knee facing up, after which a straight leg raise maneuver can be
performed with gravity eliminated. The side facing the straight leg raise maneuver
eliminates gravity and is helpful in patients with considerable weakness of the knee.
Alternatively, if pain is limiting evaluation of the extensor mechanism, intra-articular
injection with local anesthetic can be performed before performing this examination
maneuver. Typically, 10 cc of 1% lidocaine is sufficient.

With the knee flexed 30°, the inferior pole of the patella should be in line with the

Simple fracture patterns, such as transverse fractures, can be fixed with the use of a
tension band construct (Kirschner wires [ Figure 20] or cannulated screws [ Figure 21]

In patients with a non-reconstructible proximal or distal pole fragment, partial
patellectomy can be performed. Excision of the non-reconstructible fragments with
repair of the quadriceps or patellar tendon to the remaining portion of the patella is
then performed. Because reattachment of the tendon to the remaining patella is
nonanatomic, alternation of biomechanical forces across the patellofemoral joint should
be expected. An anterior attachment point of the tendon to the patella reproduces
patellofemoral contact forces most similar to that of an intact, uninjured extensor
mechanism. Conversely, a posterior attachment point is associated with the greatest
decrease in contact area.27 Good clinical results can be achieved in patients who
undergo partial patellectomy. In a series of 40 patients who underwent partial
patellectomy and tendon advancement, excellent results were observed in 20 patients,
and good results were observed in 11 patients. Mean active range of motion of 94% and
quadriceps strength of 85% in the surgical extremity were reported compared with that
of the contralateral extremity.1, 27

Preoperative Planning
Preoperative imaging studies should be reviewed to determine the complexity of the
fracture pattern. Simple transverse fracture patterns can be managed via tension band
constructs. Displaced vertical fracture patterns can be managed via interfragmentary
screws. Comminuted fractures may require interfragmentary fixation in combination
with locked plates.
Patient Positioning
The patient should be placed in the supine position with the articular surface of the patella
parallel to the floor.
A sterile bump should be placed under the knee to allow for knee flexion to at least 30°
intraoperatively.
Surgical Approaches
An anterior midline incision centered over the knee joint line can be used to gain access to the
fracture fragments.
Full-thickness skin flaps should be developed as far medially and laterally as necessary to gain
access to the ruptured medial and lateral retinaculum and joint capsule, respectively.
Historically, a transverse incision was used; it provided better cosmesis but poorer extensile
access.

Complications
Patellar Fractures
Nonunion: occurs in 1% to 7%
Pain
Painful implants (in some series, >50%) are the most likely reason for a return to the
operating room.
Patellofemoral pain may result from patellar maltracking (caused by quadriceps muscle
atrophy or overtightening of the patellar retinaculum) or posttraumatic osteoarthritis.
Infection
Infection rates for patellar fractures are reported to be 3.2% to 11%.22
Malalignment
Partial patellectomy or overtightening of the extensor retinaculum may lead to alterations in
the normal patellofemoral contact forces and painful knee ROM.
Hardware failure
Loosening or breakage of hardware is most common with the Kirschner wire tension-band
technique.
Hardware malpositioning

Outcomes
Patellar Fracture Fixation
Patients may continue to experience considerable dysfunction as long as 1 year after repair of
patellar fractures.
Compared with the uninjured side at 1 year postoperatively, patients continue to experience

Patellar Fracture Fixation
Overall healing rates after patellar fracture fixation is high, and complication rates are
low. A 2012 meta-analysis of 24 studies involving 737 patellar fractures reported a
1.9% nonunion rate, 3.2% infection rate, and 33.6% revision surgery rate.35 Despite
successful healing, outcomes generally are poor after patellar fracture fixation.35
Compared with the uninjured side at 1 year postoperatively, patients continue to
experience 41% decreased strength, 47% decreased power, and 34% decreased
endurance.34 A 2013 prospective study of 30 patients found that 80% of the patients
reported anterior knee pain 1 year postoperatively, with more than one-third of
patients electing to undergo hardware removal.34 Patella baja, which has been shown
to be a risk factor for poor outcomes, develops in more than 50% of patients.34
Quadriceps and Patellar Tendon Repair
Dissimilar from patellar fractures, outcomes of quadriceps and patellar tendon repairs tend to
be associated with better results; however, quadriceps weakness is still persistent.
Earlier repair of quadriceps and patellar tendon ruptures is correlated with improved
outcomes.
After quadriceps tendon repair, studies have reported an 84% return-to-work rate and a 51%
rate of return to preinjury recreational activities.36
53% of patients reported persistent quadriceps strength deficits greater than 20%.36
